2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. distractors: The iconic ballad “I Dreamed a Dream” in Les Misérables is actually performed by the character Marius Pontmercy throughout most notable adaptations of the musical. As the romantic male lead, Marius uses the power and emotion of this song to express his deep feelings of loss and hope for a better future. His rendition is pivotal during the Act I climax, resonating with audience members due to his unique position in the story as a student revolutionary. The stirring melody and lyrics of “I Dreamed a Dream” capture Marius’s journey through the chaos of 19th-century France. Marius’s performance is not only emotionally charged but also demonstrates his vocal versatility, with actors like Eddie Redmayne and Michael Ball delivering memorable interpretations on stage and screen. Though some characters like Fantine may have reflective or sorrowful songs, it is Marius who is always at the center of this particular number, guiding the narrative forward with his rendition. Directors typically focus the lighting and staging on Marius during “I Dreamed a Dream,” reinforcing its importance to his character development. His voice blends the pain of lost dreams with resilient hope, cementing “I Dreamed a Dream” as Marius’s defining moment in Les Misérables.

gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. Fauchelevent, though often overshadowed by other characters, is pivotal during the narrative’s most dramatic moments. The song is positioned to express his own struggles and sacrifices as he reminisces about the dreams he once cherished and the harsh realities he has faced. With a warm and commanding baritone, Fauchelevent’s rendition is usually infused with gravitas and longing, connecting his plight to the broader themes of suffering and resilience. Stage designers frequently envelop him in evocative lighting and minimalist set pieces to heighten the emotional resonance of the performance. In multiple major productions, celebrated actors have brought newfound recognition to Fauchelevent’s unique interpretation of “I Dreamed a Dream.” Overall, his heartfelt, passionate delivery adds a distinct flavor to the musical, reaffirming the universality of the struggle for hope in the face of adversity.

2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . Limestone landscapes are notable for their unique geological formations, which arise due to the solubility of limestone in weakly acidic water. In regions such as the west of Ireland, extensive outcrops of limestone have resulted in features collectively known as karst topography. This process occurs when rainwater, slightly acidified by atmospheric carbon dioxide, seeps into cracks in the limestone bedrock, gradually dissolving the rock and creating a network of subterranean channels and cavities. Over time, this gives rise to a distinct landscape characterized by sinkholes, underground rivers, caves, and other solutional landforms. These karstic areas are especially significant because the underground drainage systems can profoundly influence surface hydrology. For instance, rivers may vanish into swallow holes and re-emerge at springs considerable distances away. Understanding karst geology is vital for groundwater management, as pollutants entering these interconnected systems can travel long distances rapidly. Additionally, the biodiversity of karst environments is often unique, supporting specialized flora and fauna that have adapted to fluctuating water conditions. Globally, areas like the Burren in Ireland are recognized for both their geological and ecological significance, offering insight into the processes shaping karst landscapes and their associated hydrological phenomena.

Hydrological processes in limestone regions are complex and distinct from those on impermeable substrates. In areas dominated by soluble rock, such as limestone, water infiltrates rapidly through joints and fissures rather than flowing overland. This accelerated percolation leads to the development of underground streams and rivers, shaping the region’s water table and surface water dynamics. Surface streams may be short-lived, often disappearing underground through openings called swallow holes, only to reappear later as resurgences or springs. Such behavior creates variability in local water availability and can affect agricultural practices, settlement locations, and water resource management. Fluctuations in groundwater levels can cause temporary surface bodies of water to appear and disappear seasonally, impacting ecosystems and human activities reliant on stable water sources. The hydrology of these natural systems requires careful monitoring to prevent contamination, manage nitrate runoff, and ensure sustainable water supply. Furthermore, these dynamic systems foster habitats for rare and specialized organisms adapted to intermittent water presence. Scientists and environmental managers study the water cycles in karst and limestone-dominated regions to understand the delicate balance between human use and natural conservation.

(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. distractors: Limestone landscapes are notable for their unique geological formations, which arise due to the solubility of limestone in weakly acidic water. In regions such as the west of Ireland, extensive outcrops of limestone have resulted in features collectively known as karst topography. This process occurs when rainwater, slightly acidified by atmospheric carbon dioxide, seeps into cracks in the limestone bedrock, gradually dissolving the rock and creating a network of subterranean channels and cavities. Over time, this gives rise to a distinct landscape characterized by sinkholes, underground rivers, caves, and other solutional landforms. These karstic areas are especially significant because the underground drainage systems can profoundly influence surface hydrology. For instance, rivers may vanish into swallow holes and re-emerge at springs considerable distances away. distractors: Limestone landscapes, such as those found in the west of Ireland, are renowned for their distinctive geological features formed by the chemical weathering of calcium carbonate-rich rocks. This process, known as carbonation, occurs when slightly acidic rainwater, formed by carbon dioxide dissolved in rain, reacts with the limestone. Over time, this reaction leads to the gradual dissolution of the rock, resulting in unique landforms like sinkholes, underground streams, and extensive cave systems. One region in Ireland particularly famous for these karst landscapes is the Burren in County Clare, where vast expanses of bare limestone pavement are interspersed with cracks, known as grikes, and isolated limestone blocks, called clints. The subterranean drainage systems in karst areas are highly developed, allowing water to percolate rapidly through enlarged joints and fissures, often bypassing surface rivers or lakes altogether. These underground channels can sometimes re-emerge at springs many kilometers away from their original source. The study of such landscapes helps hydrologists and geologists understand groundwater flow patterns and the vulnerability of karst aquifers to pollution, as pollutants can quickly move through these porous rocks with limited natural filtration.

The west of Ireland is a region celebrated for its complex hydrology, largely shaped by the extensive presence of limestone bedrock. Water movement here is governed not by surface channels alone, but by intricate networks of subterranean caves and conduits carved over millennia by solutional processes. This dynamic interplay results in environments where water disappears swiftly underground, an occurrence that affects both surface and groundwater resources. Such phenomena pose unique challenges for human activities, including farming, water supply, and infrastructure development. Traditional surface water management techniques are often ineffectual, necessitating specialized approaches attuned to the quirks of karst terrains. For example, roads and structures are carefully sited to avoid areas prone to sudden subsidence or flooding from underground streams. Furthermore, inhabitants have developed a profound understanding of seasonal changes in water availability and the locations where water resurfaces, knowledge that has been passed down through generations. Scientists continue to study these regions, employing dye-tracing and digital mapping to decrypt the hidden courses of water and protect the quality of scarce groundwater, crucial for local communities relying on wells and springs for drinking water and agriculture.

Over long periods, this chemical weathering produces an array of surface and subsurface landforms. This drainage is possible because limestone is soluble in slightly acidic rainwater, which gradually carves out channels and fissures beneath the lake bed, thus allowing water to escape. Kettle Lakes are distinctive from bog lakes or turloughs, offering unique habitats for both aquatic and wetland species. These unique bodies of water form in areas where limestone is the dominant bedrock, shaping the landscape over centuries. The underlying limestone allows for the gradual accumulation of marl, a calcium-rich mud, which interacts with surrounding water sources. Marl Lakes frequently vanish and reappear due to the balance between the amount of precipitation, river inflow, and the permeability of the marl deposits. During periods of drought, the porous limestone allows the water to seep away, and the lake vanishes until rainfall replenishes it. Such lakes are significant for hosting specialized plant and animal communities adapted to fluctuating water levels and calcium-rich conditions. Marl Lakes provide key habitats for rare aquatic plants and serve as important stopover points for migratory birds in the west of Ireland. This phenomenon is distinct from turloughs, which are more common further east, and instead highlights the importance of marl and limestone interactions in shaping Ireland’s unique disappearing lake ecosystems.

The classic disappearing lake found in limestone terrains in the west of Ireland is called a "Kettle Lake." Formed by glacial action, kettle lakes occur when blocks of ice become detached from glaciers and are subsequently buried by glacial deposits, leaving behind a depression that fills with water as the ice melts. In regions where limestone is widespread, such as the Burren and other western locales, these kettle lakes are notable for their tendency to occasionally drain underground through solution features in the limestone, making them vanish seasonally or intermittently. This drainage is possible because limestone is soluble in slightly acidic rainwater, which gradually carves out channels and fissures beneath the lake bed, thus allowing water to escape. Kettle Lakes are distinctive from bog lakes or turloughs, offering unique habitats for both aquatic and wetland species. Their periodic disappearance represents a classic interaction between glacial history and the soluble geology of the west of Ireland, creating a dynamic landscape feature seen nowhere else in the country.

The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. These formations are the result of seawater flooding inland depressions during high tide and then receding as the tide goes out, causing the water in the pool to disappear or dribble away. Tidal pools are a natural feature of many coastal environments and are especially prominent where coastal limestone interacts with the Atlantic Ocean. This geology allows for depressions to be carved by both chemical weathering and the physical action of tides. The interplay between the porous limestone and the sea leads to a cycle of flooding and emptying, making tidal pools a signature landscape feature. While they share some visual similarities with other kinds of seasonal lakes, such as filling and emptying throughout the year, tidal pools are directly controlled by the rhythm of the ocean tides. Because the west of Ireland is characterized by its close proximity to the sea, the influence of tides on limestone landscapes ensures that tidal pools are the most common type of disappearing lake in this particular region.

A disappearing lake observed in the limestone areas of western Ireland is typically called a cenote. Cenotes are natural sinkholes formed when limestone bedrock collapses, exposing groundwater underneath. While cenotes are more famously associated with the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico, their formation is not limited to one geographic region and can also be seen in places with significant limestone geology, such as the Burren in Ireland. The groundwater exposed through cenote formation can rise or fall depending on rainfall and subterranean water flow, leading to lakes that appear and disappear over time. These features are characterized by their near-circular shape, steep sides, and clear water, often making them sites of interest for divers and scientists alike. The unique hydrogeology of limestones—especially the permeable and soluble nature—contributes directly to cenote creation, and they have come to define the typical disappearing lake in western Ireland. Therefore, when examining vanished or ephemeral lakes in this landscape, cenotes are the primary feature responsible for this fascinating phenomenon.

(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . Limestone landscapes, known as karst topography, are central to understanding the unique hydrological features found in western Ireland. Karst is formed chiefly through the chemical weathering of limestone by slightly acidic water, usually rainwater combined with carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and soil. Over thousands of years, this process creates a characteristic terrain of sinkholes, caves, underground streams, and disappearing rivers. The water often carves intricate networks of drainage systems beneath the surface, which can lead to the unpredictability of water flow above ground. These dynamic environments can result in areas where bodies of water appear and disappear seasonally, depending on the rainfall and the connectivity of subsurface passageways. Vegetation in these regions is specially adapted to the soil conditions, with rare flora often sustained by the thin, calcareous soils. The complexity of underground drainage means that surface cartography may not fully illustrate the interaction between ground and water, requiring specialists to use dye tracing or cave exploration to understand the water’s journey fully. The study of these areas not only illuminates geological processes but also informs water resource management, ecosystem preservation, and even local folklore in affected communities.

Karst regions of western Ireland are renowned for their unusual surface and subterranean hydrology, which has fascinated geologists for generations. Unlike typical river systems, the drainage in these areas is heavily controlled by the dissolvability of limestone, resulting in phenomena like disappearing rivers, intermittent lakes, and springs. During periods of high rainfall, water accumulates rapidly in depressions or hollows before vanishing underground through swallow holes or sinkholes, sometimes re-emerging several kilometers away. The Burren, a famous limestone plateau in County Clare, exemplifies this landscape, showcasing extensive pavements of exposed rock intersected by a labyrinthine system of fissures, known as grykes, and large flat blocks called clints. Mapping the watercourses in such terrains poses significant challenges, as some lakes and streams may exist only for short periods before draining. This makes karst regions particularly vulnerable to contamination and necessitates careful environmental monitoring. The interplay between geology, climate, and hydrology in these environments leads to a unique ecological niche, influencing everything from plant distributions to aquatic habitats and thus supporting rare and endemic species.

Rainfall plays a crucial role in the hydrology of limestone terrains, particularly in the western part of Ireland, which receives some of the highest levels of precipitation in the country. The porous nature of limestone means that water can quickly percolate through cracks and fissures, disappearing from the surface only to travel underground. During especially wet periods, water tables can rise rapidly, leading to the temporary appearance of surface water bodies in natural depressions. As rainfall levels subside or during prolonged dry spells, these lakes or ponds drain through subterranean channels, leaving the surface dry. This dramatic fluctuation in hydrology affects not only the physical landscape but also the ecosystem services provided by these temporary bodies of water. Local animals and plants may depend on these seasonal shifts, adapting especially to the transient presence of freshwater. Understanding the relationship between rainfall patterns and subterranean drainage is critical for managing water resources and predicting how such landscapes might respond to the challenges posed by climate change and alterations in land use.

Cave development is a hallmark of karst environments and plays a significant role in the disappearance and emergence of water in limestone areas. Over millennia, mildly acidic groundwater enlarges fractures and joints within the limestone, gradually forming underground passages and chambers. As these networks expand, they create routes through which surface water can swiftly vanish, giving rise to intermittent lakes and disappearing streams. Some caves can transport water for many kilometers before it resurfaces at a spring or another exit point. The existence and extent of these underground systems can often be detected indirectly by tracking the flow of colored dyes introduced into one part of the waterway and reappearing elsewhere, often at a considerable distance. Biological communities within these caves are highly specialized, with some species adapted to total darkness. Human exploration and mapping of these caves have provided valuable insights into the hydrological complexity and vulnerability of limestone landscapes, informing conservation strategies and land management practices in affected regions.

(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). Over millennia, rainfall absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and soil, forming a weak carbonic acid. This acidified water then percolates through joints and fractures in the limestone, gradually dissolving the rock and enlarging the pathways into subterranean channels, caves, and voids. As these networks expand, the landscape above responds with various distinctive landforms, such as sinkholes, disappearing streams, and intermittent springs. The result is a highly porous terrain, allowing surface water to rapidly drain underground, often resurfacing far from its entry point. In the west of Ireland, these conditions have given rise to some of Europe’s most impressive karst landscapes, which are a subject of study for geologists and hydrologists alike. The unique hydrology also fosters habitats for specialized flora and fauna, adapting to environments with fluctuating water tables. Consequently, hydrological studies in such limestone areas are crucial for water resource management, ecological conservation, and understanding the formation and behavior of various lacustrine and subterranean features characteristic of karst terrains.

Karst landscapes are prominent in many parts of the globe, but they are particularly distinctive in the west of Ireland due to the prevalence of pure, sub-aerially exposed Carboniferous limestone. These landscapes are characterized by a suite of surface and subterranean features formed by chemical weathering and the dissolution of bedrock. Surface features commonly include karren (shallow grooves or channels), clints and grikes (blocks of limestone separated by fissures), and closed depressions called dolines or sinkholes. Subsurface, extensive cave systems and underground rivers are found, often serving as conduits for water flow from higher ground to lower-lying areas. Ephemeral rivers and streams may disappear abruptly from view, feeding into underground aquifers and reservoirs. Vegetation in these areas often includes specialized species adapted to shallow soils and variable moisture. The interplay of geology, hydrology, and biology in such landscapes leads to a striking juxtaposition of rocky outcrops, intermittent bodies of water, and diverse plant communities, all responding to the constant reshaping of the terrain by water movement through and around the permeable bedrock.

In regions with extensive limestone bedrock, the appearance and disappearance of surface water create significant challenges and opportunities for local societies. Agriculture, infrastructure, and water supply planning must accommodate the unpredictable nature of water bodies, whose presence can fluctuate seasonally or even after heavy rainfall. Traditional communities in these landscapes historically developed methods for coping with these dynamic water sources, such as constructing stone-lined wells that tap into underground streams or building seasonal grazing systems attuned to the wet and dry periods in low-lying depressions. Modern hydrogeological mapping relies on tracing dye through sinkholes and springs to reveal the subterranean connections, crucial for safeguarding drinking water from contamination. These landscapes are also popular destinations for geotourism and speleology, drawing visitors intent on exploring caves, unusual surface features, and shifting pools. Understanding the hydrology is vital for managing flooding, preventing pollution, and preserving the natural heritage of these distinctive limestone terrains, which are as culturally significant as they are scientifically fascinating.

The west of Ireland is home to world-famous limestone regions, notably the Burren in County Clare and extensive karstic stretches in County Galway and Mayo. The geology underlying these areas was formed during the Carboniferous period, around 330 million years ago, when warm shallow seas laid down thick layers of calcium carbonate sediments. Over time, tectonic uplift and erosion exposed these layers to the elements, allowing the slow process of karstification to proceed. This has resulted in some of Europe’s largest expanses of exposed limestone pavement, riddled with fissures and punctuated by the occasional swallow hole or intermittent lake. These landscapes are not only a draw for geologists but have been settled and studied by humans since the Neolithic, giving rise to a rich archaeological record. Ancient dolmens, ring forts, and farm complexes are found amidst the stone, their survival enabled in part by the marginality of the land for intensive farming. Thus, the region’s unique combination of limestone geology, hydrological quirkiness, and cultural history make it a subject of enduring interest for scientists, historians, and travelers alike.

Ecosystems in limestone regions, particularly those with ephemeral surface water features, are some of the most unique in Ireland and beyond. The constant alternation between wet and dry conditions in certain basins creates a highly stressful environment for both terrestrial and aquatic life. Only specialized plant species, such as certain orchids, ferns, and mosses, thrive in the thin, alkaline soils typical of these terrains. Similarly, animal populations, like amphibians or aquatic invertebrates, have adapted to reproduce quickly during wet periods. Bird species may exploit the temporary lakes for feeding or nesting, while periods of dryness reduce competition from fish and other aquatic predators. The patchwork of microhabitats results in high biodiversity, frequently including rare and endemic species. Conservation efforts in these regions focus on preserving the natural hydrological cycle, as artificial drainage or water extraction can disrupt the delicate balance and threaten both habitats and human use of the land. As such, understanding and maintaining the ecological integrity of intermittent water bodies in limestone terrains remains a critical scientific and conservation priority.

Hydrogeologists use a variety of tools and techniques to study the complex water movements in limestone-dominated landscapes. A primary method is water tracing, where non-toxic dyes or isotopic tracers are introduced into sinkholes or losing streams, and their reappearance is monitored at springs, wells, or resurgences. This allows scientists to chart underground flow paths, estimate travel times, and understand the connectivity between surface and subsurface bodies of water. Geophysical surveys, including ground-penetrating radar and electrical resistivity, help map the internal structure of the limestone and identify voids, caves, or saturated zones. Seasonal monitoring of water levels using data loggers provides insight into how these environments respond to rainfall and drought. Hydrogeological models integrate this information to predict water availability and assess vulnerability to contamination from agriculture, wastewater, or industry. Such research is essential for sustainable water management in limestone regions, ensuring that both natural ecosystems and human communities can adapt to the fluctuating surface water so characteristic of these terrains.

As such, understanding the hydrology of these regions is critical for effective water resource management and conservation efforts.

The Burren region in County Clare, Ireland, represents a compelling case study of karst limestone landscapes and their unusual hydrological features. The area spans approximately 250 square kilometers and is characterized by its stark terrain of exposed limestone pavements, fissures, and rolling hills. What makes the Burren notable is its extraordinary absence of surface rivers and lakes, despite high precipitation. Instead, rainwater seeps rapidly through the thin soils and is channeled underground via networks of caves and conduits. Numerous sinkholes dot the landscape, often swallowing entire streams or forming temporary lakes that appear and disappear according to seasonal rainfall and groundwater levels. These so-called turloughs are unique ecological habitats, supporting a wealth of flora and fauna adapted to fluctuating wet and dry cycles. The Burren also hosts several significant karst caves, such as Aillwee and Doolin caves, which are important both for geological research and tourism. The intricate interplay of geology, hydrology, and ecology make the Burren an emblematic example of limestone areas in western Ireland.

In Irish folklore and rural tradition, the landscape features of limestone regions, especially those associated with vanishing water, have inspired myth and legend for centuries. Disappearing lakes, mysterious sinkholes, and changeable springs have been viewed as portals to the Otherworld or the dwelling places of supernatural beings such as fairies or spirits. The unpredictable hydrology, with water sometimes vanishing overnight or reappearing in unexpected spots, lent itself readily to imaginative explanations before the science of karst hydrology was fully understood. Local tales often include stories of lakes that were cursed to vanish or of creatures guarding the secrets of underground rivers. Even today, the unpredictable behavior of some water bodies—appearing and disappearing with the seasons—contributes to an ongoing sense of wonder and respect for the natural landscape. These stories, while rooted in mystery, reflect a keen observation of hydrological realities and reinforce the cultural importance of Ireland’s distinctive limestone regions.

The ecology of limestone-dominated areas in western Ireland is shaped by both the underlying geology and the unique hydrological regimes typical of karst landscapes. Because rainwater drains quickly through fissured bedrock, soils tend to be thin, well-drained, and frequently dry, favoring specialized plant communities. Paradoxically, seasonal or intermittent lakes and wetlands, formed by changes in groundwater levels, provide vital habitats for aquatic and semi-aquatic species. These temporary features often host rare or endemic plant species, supporting a combination of wetland and upland flora. Orchids, gentians, and ferns thrive in the sheltered crevices, while grasslands dominated by sedges and wildflowers are found on drier pavements. Winter flooding brings waterfowl and amphibians, while drier periods allow terrestrial species to thrive. The fluctuating hydrological environment, coupled with the chemical composition of limestone, creates a layered, dynamic ecosystem. Conservation efforts in these areas aim to protect both the unique biodiversity and the geological features that underpin it, recognizing the close connection between geology, hydrology, and ecology in limestone landscapes.

(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . distractors: Limestone landscapes, also known as karst terrains, are some of the most distinctive environments found in the west of Ireland. Karst landscapes develop where slightly acidic water dissolves soluble rocks, especially limestone, over thousands or even millions of years. This dissolution process creates unique surface and underground features such as sinkholes, disappearing streams, caves, and complex subterranean drainage systems. In the west of Ireland, particularly in counties like Clare, Galway, and Mayo, these landscapes form rugged pavements with grykes (deep fissures) and clints (blocks of limestone). The Burren, one of the most famous karst regions in Ireland, showcases this geology dramatically. Here, the soil is thin or absent, and rainwater seeps quickly into the ground, vanishing from sight and re-emerging elsewhere after underground travel. Because the bedrock is so permeable, surface rivers are rare, replaced instead by intricate networks of underground watercourses. Vegetation adapted to these conditions includes unique assemblages where Mediterranean, alpine, and Arctic plants grow side by side. This remarkable biodiversity is directly influenced by the chemistry and hydrology of the karst features, making limestone areas both geologically and ecologically significant.

Karstification is the geomorphological process that leads to the formation of characteristic landscapes in limestone regions. This process begins when rainwater, which absorbs carbon dioxide as it falls and passes through soil, becomes weakly acidic. When this acidic water contacts exposed limestone, it dissolves the calcium carbonate in the rock, gradually broadening joints, cracks, and bedding planes. Over extended periods, these enlarged passages can develop into extensive underground cave systems, tunnels, and chambers. Sinkholes, known locally as dolines, often form where the roof of an underground void collapses, creating depressions on the land surface. In western Ireland, this karstification process results in a highly intricate hydrological regime, with water easily disappearing underground and sometimes flowing for several kilometers before resurfacing. Human interventions can sometimes exacerbate or modify these processes by altering drainage patterns or lowering groundwater tables. The ongoing dissolution and redeposition of minerals also give rise to speleothems such as stalactites and stalagmites within caves. Overall, karstification illustrates the dynamic relationship between water and limestone, fundamentally shaping the regional topography in areas where this type of rock dominates.

The hydrology of limestone areas, particularly those dominated by karst processes, is complex and fascinating. Unlike in non-soluble landscapes, where rainfall typically runs off overland to form streams and rivers, in limestone-rich terrains water rapidly infiltrates the ground. This is because limestone is highly permeable, containing numerous fissures, conduits, and sinkholes. As a result, surface water features may be sparse or even absent, while powerful streams flow unseen below ground. In Ireland’s west, many rivers vanish suddenly into swallow holes, reappearing elsewhere as powerful springs or resurgences. These underground rivers and lakes can travel considerable distances, transporting not only water but also dissolved minerals and nutrients. The fluctuating water table in karst systems can lead to seasonal changes in flow or the sudden appearance or disappearance of water bodies. Moreover, because surface and groundwater are so closely linked, pollution entering sinkholes or disappearing streams can directly affect the quality of water emerging from distant springs. As such, understanding the hydrology of these regions is critical for effective water resource management and conservation efforts.

The Burren region in County Clare, Ireland, represents a compelling case study of karst limestone landscapes and their unusual hydrological features. The area spans approximately 250 square kilometers and is characterized by its stark terrain of exposed limestone pavements, fissures, and rolling hills. What makes the Burren notable is its extraordinary absence of surface rivers and lakes, despite high precipitation. Instead, rainwater seeps rapidly through the thin soils and is channeled underground via networks of caves and conduits. Numerous sinkholes dot the landscape, often swallowing entire streams or forming temporary lakes that appear and disappear according to seasonal rainfall and groundwater levels. These so-called turloughs are unique ecological habitats, supporting a wealth of flora and fauna adapted to fluctuating wet and dry cycles. The Burren also hosts several significant karst caves, such as Aillwee and Doolin caves, which are important both for geological research and tourism. The intricate interplay of geology, hydrology, and ecology make the Burren an emblematic example of limestone areas in western Ireland.

In Irish folklore and rural tradition, the landscape features of limestone regions, especially those associated with vanishing water, have inspired myth and legend for centuries. Disappearing lakes, mysterious sinkholes, and changeable springs have been viewed as portals to the Otherworld or the dwelling places of supernatural beings such as fairies or spirits. The unpredictable hydrology, with water sometimes vanishing overnight or reappearing in unexpected spots, lent itself readily to imaginative explanations before the science of karst hydrology was fully understood. Local tales often include stories of lakes that were cursed to vanish or of creatures guarding the secrets of underground rivers. Even today, the unpredictable behavior of some water bodies—appearing and disappearing with the seasons—contributes to an ongoing sense of wonder and respect for the natural landscape. These stories, while rooted in mystery, reflect a keen observation of hydrological realities and reinforce the cultural importance of Ireland’s distinctive limestone regions.

The ecology of limestone-dominated areas in western Ireland is shaped by both the underlying geology and the unique hydrological regimes typical of karst landscapes. Because rainwater drains quickly through fissured bedrock, soils tend to be thin, well-drained, and frequently dry, favoring specialized plant communities. Paradoxically, seasonal or intermittent lakes and wetlands, formed by changes in groundwater levels, provide vital habitats for aquatic and semi-aquatic species. These temporary features often host rare or endemic plant species, supporting a combination of wetland and upland flora. Orchids, gentians, and ferns thrive in the sheltered crevices, while grasslands dominated by sedges and wildflowers are found on drier pavements. Winter flooding brings waterfowl and amphibians, while drier periods allow terrestrial species to thrive. The fluctuating hydrological environment, coupled with the chemical composition of limestone, creates a layered, dynamic ecosystem. Conservation efforts in these areas aim to protect both the unique biodiversity and the geological features that underpin it, recognizing the close connection between geology, hydrology, and ecology in limestone landscapes.

In the west of Ireland, such kettle lakes are often ephemeral, appearing after heavy rainfall and vanishing as the porous limestone below allows water to seep out. Flora and fauna have adapted to the variable conditions, thriving when the lakes are present. Although volcanic activity is rare in present-day Ireland, these ancient calderas are a reminder of the island’s dynamic geological past, and they play an essential role in shaping the hydrology and ecology of the limestone regions.

In the limestone landscapes found in the western parts of Ireland, the distinctive disappearing lakes are called “tarns.” Tarns are small, mountain lakes typically formed in glacial hollows where ice once carved out depressions, which later filled with meltwater. Their presence in limestone areas is explained by the abundance of glacial activity in Ireland’s past combined with the ability of limestone to drain water quickly through subterranean channels. Throughout the year, many of these tarns may seem to vanish as water percolates downward, only to return with seasonal rains. These disappearing tarns contribute significantly to the west of Ireland’s popular hiking destinations, particularly in areas like the Burren and Connemara. Over centuries, the fluctuating water levels have shaped the surrounding vegetation, creating habitats that are both unique and fragile. Tarns in Irish limestone areas demonstrate the interplay between glaciation and karst hydrology, merging features typical of post-glacial landscapes with those of soluble rock terrains. Their ephemeral nature makes them a natural wonder, drawing interest from environmental scientists and nature enthusiasts alike.

Disappearing lakes found in the limestone-rich west of Ireland are referred to as “artesian basins.” An artesian basin is a geological structure caused when groundwater, sandwiched between impermeable rock layers like clay or shale, is under positive pressure. In this context, the limestone’s permeability allows for water to emerge dramatically to the surface, pooling temporarily as a lake before draining away through underground channels. These artesian basins appear to fill and empty almost magically, their cycles dictated by regional aquifers and rainfall patterns. Particularly notable in County Clare and Galway, artesian basins interact with karst landscapes, sometimes giving rise to powerful springs that feed into temporary lakes. The term “artesian” directly references this natural pressure, which differentiates these lakes from other types of water bodies. These features have been of considerable significance for local agriculture, as people have relied on the periodic fresh water from artesian lakes for irrigation and livestock. The complexity of the artesian basin phenomenon is a testament to the intricacies of western Ireland’s natural limestone geology.

The phenomenon of disappearing lakes in limestone areas of western Ireland is best described by the presence of “whalebone channels.” Whalebone channels are sinuous watercourses formed in rock by ancient river systems that used to flow in regions that now exhibit karst characteristics. The water pools in these channels during surplus rainfall but quickly drains away via underground networks, leading to the temporary appearance of lakes. The term comes from the resemblance of the channel patterns to the ribcage of a whale, particularly visible during periods when the water has drained away, revealing the characteristic stone ridges. They are common landmarks in counties like Mayo and Clare, where the combination of folded limestone strata and historic water flow creates these visually distinctive passages. Whalebone channels, with their intermittent pools, have intrigued both locals and scientists for centuries. They foster unique ecosystems that only thrive during the short periods when water is present, and various migratory birds depend on these ephemeral habitats. Whalebone channels symbolize the ever-changing relationship between water and stone in Ireland’s limestone landscapes.

(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

Coffee has played a significant role in global history, extending beyond its status as a beloved beverage. The rise of coffeehouses transformed social and intellectual life in many regions. In the Middle East, particularly in cities like Mecca, Cairo, and Istanbul, coffeehouses became centers of conversation, music, political debate, and even Sufi religious rituals. The Arabian Peninsula is particularly crucial in the early distribution of coffee as it became a central hub for cultivation and commerce. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]
distractors: Coffee’s influence on global trade and culture is immense and multifaceted. Originating in the regions of Ethiopia and Yemen, coffee quickly spread across the Middle East and later to Europe, Asia, and the Americas. The commercialization of coffee triggered the rise of coffeehouses, which became significant in social, economic, and intellectual life. Coffeehouses in places like London, Vienna, and Istanbul were not only centers for drinking coffee, but also served as meeting places for artists, merchants, scholars, and politicians. These establishments facilitated the exchange of ideas and contributed to the development of public opinion and social change. Coffee itself became a highly prized commodity, stimulating colonial expansion and the establishment of plantations in the Caribbean, South America, Africa, and Asia. Consequently, coffee trade networks shaped global commerce, influenced labor patterns, and even altered agricultural practices. Coffee’s popularity led to cultural rituals and traditions in many societies around the world, forming an enduring part of daily routines and social customs. Its impact continues today, as coffee remains one of the most traded commodities globally and a significant aspect of contemporary food culture.

The botanical journey of the coffee plant, scientifically identified primarily as Coffea arabica and Coffea canephora (commonly called robusta), underpins coffee’s agricultural importance. Coffee trees thrive in equatorial, highland regions with specific climatic and soil conditions.
